The reason why I mention that again is that I think there is a system on the part of the contractors, recognizing that these things are not too closely checked, that when government engineers estimate that a project should cost, say $100,000, one contractor puts in a bid of $96,000, another $92,000, the lowest tenderer gets it, and I am safe in saying that on the basis of this airport return, when the project is completed it will probably cost twice the amount of the lowest tender. I think they are deliberately underbidding because they know that the precedent has been set; that they are not too closely checked and that they can throw in another building here and there and make money out of the job. I know the minister's department is very competent. I know he has not the time himself to scrutinize all these matters with the care required. I am in hopes that the recently appointed committee on war expenditures will pay strict attention to the manner of letting contracts, because from evidence we have had from time to time I am reasonably sure that things are not as they should be. I am not blaming the minister for that. There is no individual who could check that matter as closely as it should be checked.
The next matter I wish to bring to his attention is wartime housing. I am not going into it from the national aspect, but I shall refer briefly to the housing situation in Sydney. As I have pointed out from time to time I. think the Dominion Steel and Coal corporation are practically running the province of Nova Scotia. In a return I had of correspondence that passed between the city of Sydney and the department on the question of wartime housing I know the situation is bad. Anyone residing in that city knows it. Perhaps 1,000 additional men have gone to the steel plant. In addition, the plate mill, when going at capacity, will employ 400 to' 600 men. Many public works projects have been undertaken in that area. There is a big one now in progress at Point Edward just across the harbour. There are thousands of men in the city and area that were not there

when the war broke out. I notice in this correspondence between the city of Sydney and the Department of Munitions and Supply that the city had no say with the representative who was sent there to make a probe. He spent twenty-four hours in the city, and I think he spent twenty-three of those hours with Dominion Steel and Coal corporation officials. The officials of the city of Sydney were ignored absolutely. According to this return the whole report is based on the fact that this man was advised by the officials of the Dominion Steel and Coal corporation that wartime housing was not necessary, that there was no importation of labour, that practically everyone employed in the war industries there was taken from local labour. That is not true. I know that from Inverness county, Richmond county and other parts of Nova Scotia and other parts of the country, many men have come into the city to work in war industries, aggravating the housing situation. There are also thousands of merchant seamen in the port, and there is also a large airport. Airmen from all over Canada are coming there with their wives, and hunting all over for a place where they can stay.
The report states: "We are not responsible for the influx of people belonging to the army, navy" and so forth. Technically they may not be, but certainly it should be someone's responsibility to provide homes for those in the armed forces. Those employed in industry are very likely going to stay there and they have an incentive to build their own homes, but the men in the armed forces are not going to build homes for themselves, and accordingly they rent. There is no control over the renting of rooms, and prices are terrible. There are wholesale evictions in that city. I suggest that in future when a representative of wartime housing is sent to make an examination of the requirements of a city he should secure his information from those who are responsible for the civic administration. Dominion Steel and Coal corporation are not affected by these wholesale evictions, but the mayor and council are, and they are badly affected at the present time. I may be suspicious, but at all events I am of opinion that the company wish to have a clear field for themselves, because they are in the housing game. They have thousands of houses-
Shacks.

Yes; they are not houses, but the company are getting rents and profits from them, and are endeavouring to keep the field clear for themselves.

War Appropriation-Supplies
There is another point I wish to make in that connection. Apart from the fact that the houses put up by wartime housing are a waste of money, they are not constructed properly and will be tom down after the war. They will not stand longer than ten years. If wartime housing is a project to enable those employed in industry to have a house fit to live in, the houses should be constructed properly, and furthermore $26 and $30 a month rent is too much to ask a working man to pay because the great majority of them cannot afford to pay that much. If the government is going to put up simply shacks for the duration of the war, it might as well put up tents, and then there would not be so much money wasted, as there will be when these houses are tom down after the war. I am really ashamed of that project. I have been in some of these houses in Halifax and Dartmouth, and if the minister happens to visit the island of Cape Breton I should like him to look at the homes that are being built there under a cooperative plan for around $1,800. They have complete radiation, six rooms, and they are being built by the people themselves in groups. If the average contractor were to erect a house of that kind, he would ask not less than $6,000, but the people who are putting up these houses cooperatively are doing the job themselves for $1,800. There are five groups building their own little village on that basis. If the minister will then look at the houses in this wartime housing project, he will see the difference, and I think he will get that cooperative group, instead of Wartime Housing, to put up the houses in future. Wartime housing is, in my opinion, an absolute waste of money.
I have read many documents and listened to many speeches since the outbreak of war, and I have heard economists on the radio and in committees making speeches, all stressing the fact that if we are going to build for the future, any housing project undertaken now should be related to our peacetime economy, with a view to the houses being used after the war. Just the opposite is true of wartime housing. I was very much encouraged to sit on the rehabilitation and reconstruction committee. I think the government has chosen excellent men -who are writing excellent reports, but what is actually being done does not dovetail with those reports at all.
Another matter I would bring to the minister's attention is the need for a greater utilization of our resources. There are deposits of dolomite at New Campbellton in Nova Scotia on the Cape Breton island end. I have here quite an article about it which appeared in the Halifax Herald. Evidently
there was some work going on there; at one time the government were interested in it, and it was expected that an industry would be established there and that dolomite could be used for machine tools and so forth. But our government apparently lost interest in it. Then some United States firm became interested in it, but later dropped out. If the minister does not know anything about this matter, I shall be glad to send him this clipping. I do not want to read it because it is lengthy. The matter is important, however, and some people are very much disappointed that the development is not being gone ahead with.
To turn to another matter, officers in the army certainly seem to require some very elaborate furnishings. Recently in Halifax I was handed a duplicate invoice from the T. Eaton Company Limited for thp fitting up of officers' quarters and, according to this, there are rugs on the floor costing as high as $195 apiece.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Who is paying for them?
The Department of Munitions and Supply. I will give the minister this invoice.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The officers furnish their
own mess.

This invoice bills the
Department of Munitions and Supply, and I see that one rug costs $195; another, $130.50; another, $214.75, and another, $130. The total bill is $746.25 for rugs.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Will the hon. member send
the invoice over to me, please?
Yes. I do not know whether this expenditure can be justified, but it certainly seems exorbitant to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I should like to see the bill.

I will send it over to the
minister and he might check up on it.
I do not want to occupy any more time, but I felt I had to make these few observations. I realize that no minister is able to keep track of all these matters himself, and when some members rise in their places and deprecate the fact that other members take up the time of the house, I say that there is not enough time for members to take up provided that they utilize it in the proper way. There are 245 members of this house. My opinion is that each one of them is responsible for a certain section of the country, and it is his job to do a job for that section. If there is anything that is not right, it is the member's job to assist the minister in correcting what is wrong. I think each
War Appropriation-Supplies

and every member, if he does his job conscientiously, can be the greatest asset any minister or government can have through the cooperation members can give in making constructive suggestions-not merely criticizing for political purposes.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) drew attention to a memorandum on steel put out by the steel workers' organizing committee. I suggest that every hon. member should read it, because I understand all have it. It would be interesting to some of our hon. friends who from time to time make the statement that the C.I.O. is a sabotaging organization, or something of that sort. The committee to which I refer took the trouble to send their national director across the country to every steel plant in order to meet the ^employees of those steel plants. I happened to have the privilege of sitting in with them at Sydney, when the memorandum was being prepared. The men in the plant, through the medium of their unions, or through whatever medium he could reach them, have attempted to find out if ways and means could be devised to meet the steel situation. They know much better than we do that there is a shortage, and that it is going to continue. I saw the director sit in with these union committees, and organize production committees of men in the plants, to devise ways and means on the job of improving the situation.
I should like to draw attention to the significance of scrap material. They point out very definitely in their memorandum that to the average man scrap is just junk, and serves no useful purpose. In the last analysis, however, it is found that it is one of the most important war materials we shall have to get. They point out that in 1939 Canada's foundries and furnaces used 1,293,877 tons of scrap and that in 1940 they used 1,819,162 tons. To put it even more strikingly, 65-8 per cent of the materials which went into the foundries in 1940 was scrap, and of all the ingredients used in the steel furnaces during the year 55 per cent was scrap. Thus the proper collection and distribution of available scrap becomes of vital importance to our war effort.
I do not wish to read all the memorandum, because it would take too much time. I would point out, however, that they make definite recommendations with respect to the organization of committees to gather scrap, and to see that it is placed in the hands of those who need it. They indicate one very pertinent fact, that one plant-it is located

in Nova Scotia-has two years supply of scrap material ahead, while another plant has only seven weeks supply. They recommend that some organization be set up to distribute that scrap material to those sections where it is essential, and where there is a shortage of it. There is no reason why one plant should have a two years supply, and another plant a supply which would last only seven weeks. The plant with only the seven weeks supply will either close down or be put on short 'ime. Amherst is an example of that. It has been closed for some time, although it may be operating to-day; I am not sure. It was, however, closed down for the want of scrap material, despite the fact that another plant has a supply sufficient for two years. Amherst should have had some of that scrap.
There is no doubt that large quantities of scrap across the country are not being salvaged. There are thousands of tons of steel rails in the different cities of Canada. The cost of reclaiming this might be a little high, but it could be salvaged. I know that around coal mines in Nova Scotia there are thousands and thousands of tons of scrap, which is not being salvaged at all. In fact, in the mines there are thousands of tons which could be taken out and used. I have in mind one mine which has been closed up and, as far as I know, has not been used for some time. I know of an old mine in Inverness county, the Mabou mine, which was operated thirty years ago, and in which there are a couple of miles of rails. Someone by the name of Stewart in New Glasgow has an option on that mine. He is not doing anything with those rails, and he has refused to allow anybody to lift them. It seems to me that they are still there; at least they were there last summer, because I was there and saw them.
In view of the necessity for raw material and for scrap to-day, nothing like that should stand in our way. If scrap is needed, then the fact that someone holds a piece of paper written in 1895, or some such time, giving him an equity in those rails, is no reason why that paper should hold good. That material belongs to the country; it is necessary and it should be taken. However, I shall not say any more about that, because the minister has the report.
There are many recommendations made in the report of that organization. They are practical recommendations and, if applied, will solve the scrap and other problems. I should hope that they would be considered by those who are directing the war effort. The steel

War Appropriation-Supplies
workers' organizing committee ought to be commended for the time they took and the money they spent in bringing that material together. I know for a fact that the director travelled across the country.
I now come to the rationing of gasoline in the maritime provinces. I heard the minister's statement, and I realize the necessity for what is being done there. If we cannot get gasoline there, then we shall have to ration what is available. My suggestion to the minister is that all the available gasoline in the maritime provinces should be rationed on the basis that every non-essential car be taken off the road. Seventy-five per cent of the gasoline being used in Canada is, in my opinion, being used only for pleasure driving. Anyone who may be travelling on the roads at two or three or four o'clock in the morning knows that there are thousands of cars travelling back and forth that are certainly not performing a useful service as far as the country is concerned. If war is as serious as people say it is, and as I know it is, then this should be our first consideration. I do not consider it any hardship to walk a mile or two miles to my work. I drove a car for twenty-two years, but I have not taken the wheel of one since war broke out, and I do not intend to.
The basis that I have suggested is the one on which gasoline should be rationed, if there is a shortage. But if we are going to be rough and tough about the matter, then we shall have to be absolutely certain that no favouritism is shown. What about commercial travellers and insurance agents, who are in a special category? A car is not necessary to an insurance agent, any more than it is to me-and probably not as much. Cars are not essential to insurance agents, because their districts are not so very large that they cannot be travelled on foot or by other conveyances. They always did that, until a few years ago. I do not think it is too great a sacrifice to ask of them; it will do them good, and make them healthy.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: While they are in a special class, they must show necessity before they get anything better than category A. They may make a case for themselves, but I believe only a small proportion are getting better than category A.

There are homes in which there are two or three cars in one family, all holding ration books. That is something which should be curtailed. I have received telegrams in protest against the curtailment of gasoline in the maritimes, and I have some understanding of the situation. If the gasoline is not there in sufficient quantities, then we shall have to ration what we have. As I said a moment ago, however, the rationing should be done on a basis of essentiality. One man
may want more than two gallons, whereas another man who really does not need his car is wasting gasoline by running it. Until the basis I have suggested is adopted, the government will have trouble. I am sorry to have taken up so much time, but I did want to make these observations.

Mr. Chairman, I had prepared an address which was to have taken the whole forty minutes, but after the remarks of the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair), I have condensed it from forty minutes to four minutes. I do not intend to make any general remarks because this has been attended to quite well by other speakers, but I do want to bring two or three suggestions to the attention of the minister, and I do not do this in any critical spirit. Notwithstanding any remarks to the contrary, and for the most part they have been given in a fine spirit, I want to congratulate the minister upon the full, frank and exhaustive resume which he has given of the work of his department. That department started not long ago from scratch, and in a marvellously short time it has built up all across this country an edifice of which the average Canadian citizen is not fully aware. It has done this with a speed and with a degree of stability that is simply astounding to those who study what has been done-600 contracts in a day, 400 planes in a month, 600,000 Canadian citizens working in war-time production. That is the record of which any minister might well be proud. As I said, however, I did not rise to speak in general terms.
A few days ago I received a resolution which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. This was adopted by the rural municipality of Daly, Manitoba. I think I know all the members of this rural council, and they are not the critical type. They desire to help, and anything they say in this resolution is with that end in view. We keep coming back to this gasoline question, which is a burning question in more respects than one. The resolution reads:
Whereas farmers are not allowed to buy gasoline by the barrel under the oil ration regulations and in numerous eases must travel many miles to procure same, thereby losing valuable working hours and wasting gas travelling to and from town unnecessarily, therefore the council of the rural municipality of Daly respectfully request the oil controller to allow farmers to buy gasoline by the barrel as heretofore, having the coupons deleted from their ration books, which action would prove a saving on gasoline and allow farmers more time to attend to their farming operations.
Respectfully submitted.
Some of these things may not appear important to many hon. members, but with respect to rural conditions they are o-f prime

War Appropriation-Supplies

importance. These men are all short-handed for farm labour, which is also an important question. In many instances farmers have to leave their work on the farm, go perhaps two or three miles to their homes, prepare for their trip into town, take a chance when they go out to their cars on having a flat tire because of the poor quality of tires now being used, try to get into town at least half an hour before the closing hour, and then find a congestion of other cars waiting to be served. They would like to be able to buy gasoline by the barrel against their coupons, and I am placing their request before the minister.
There is another matter, one which I think has been raised by other hon. members. I have received a good many letters urging that some change be made in the regulations so that farmers can go in and buy gasoline at least two evenings in the week at an hour later than that prescribed by the regulations. The farmers find they have to lose too much time when they must reach the station before the present closing hour. As I say, they are not making this suggestion in any critical spirit; it is only in an effort to conserve time and gasoline, which is, I think, a most praiseworthy motive.
Another suggestion I have to make is that the department take some steps to see to it that certain service station operators and many of those in other lines of business who have been practically put out of business because of the present regulations should be taken care of in some other line of work. These people have claims upon the public; they have built up their business over a term of years, and some of them are now forced to close their doors. There is other work that most of these men can do to advantage, and I suggest that in any openings which may be available they be not subject to the regulations of the civil service commission. In saying that, I am casting no reflection upon that commission; I have no reason to do so, but I think the tests should be reliability and ability to do the job. Any man who can pass these two tests should get preference.
I was glad to hear the minister say that as far as possible smaller companies, garages and others who have suffered severely because of certain restrictions, will be given every preference possible. I have always been a believer, and I am more so to-day, in the decentralization of industry. I do not think it is a healthy condition for any country to have its industries centralized. I am glad to know that the minister is aware of the advisability of taking care of these smaller institutions as far as is practicable. That is all I have to say.
I Mr. Matthews.]
First, I suggest that our farmers should be put to the least possible inconvenience in filling their gasoline requirements. Second, I suggest that service station operators who are suffering because of the present regulations be given some preference whenever the occasion offers. Third, I suggest that the smaller repair and manufacturing companies in this country be given an advantage wherever possible over the larger centres of industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I have a brief statement to make which perhaps I should have made before. A number of hon. members have suggested that provision be made in rural areas to permit gasoline stations to remain open in the evenings for the convenience of farmers. I may say that arrangements have been completed whereby gas stations five miles distant from a city will be authorized to keep open one evening a week. Arrangements can probably be made so that gasoline will be available two or three evenings a week to farmers coming into town.
Will that be only for farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: It will be available to anyone who comes along.
What about purchasing by the barrel?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That cannot be done.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion with respect to the minister's work and his share of this $2,000,000,000 appropriation. I am not by any means satisfied that our resources are being used to the degree to which they could be used. I am not disposed to find fault with the minister.
I think he attempted a colossal task, a task probably beyond the power of any one human being, and I believe that he has wrestled with it heroically. I may not be deemed, in saying that, a very good opposition member, but I do not see why a man should not have a little credit when he has earned it. At the same time it is well for us to bear in mind that there is in our keeping, perhaps right in this chamber, perhaps in the minister's department, the future of six hundred and fifty million people-the people of the whole British empire and of the United States. If we fail to produce the armoured cars-the tanks, the aeroplanes and the other necessities of war to the degree to which we can produce them, in whatever degree we fall short we shall jeopardize the future of all those free peoples who constitute our friends.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I am not at all satisfied with respect to the gasoline matter. I simply cannot be convinced that everything has been done which could be done to provide this country with gasoline and other fuel. I firmly believe that there are people, organizations, with ulterior motives, deliberately preventing the development of the fuel supply of this country, blocking the efforts of the minister to produce the maximum.
The committee which the minister mentioned, which has been selected from his own department to examine into the possibility of producing oil from the Athabaska sands, should be able to get right to work and produce results, and produce them quickly. This business of dawdling along, waiting until next year, hoping that the war will end before they have to produce oil, is not to be tolerated. That is exactly how I feel about the matter. I do not think the committee is on its job. I do not believe it is producing results. As we say out in the west, "I don't believe it is cutting the mustard." I think it ought to be told to get right to work and make a report soon. I should like to know who these committee people are, and when they are to hand in their report. What is it about the Athabaska tar sands that they do not now know? They have been studying the 'Athabaska tar sands for many years. Voluminous reports are to be had. What they do not know, it seems to me they could find out very soon if they chose to do so. The minister, in his reply to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol), spoke of a number of problems, but very vaguely. I do not see why those problems could not be detailed to this committee so that we could know exactly what they are. One is likely, of course, to hear rumours that are not entirely correct; nevertheless I do not think that all is well with the Athabaska tar sands situation.
The minister mentioned that he had taken into counsel certain companies and is expecting them to advise him whether it is well to go ahead. Has the minister chosen companies which can be entirely trusted? There are some companies, from whom I certainly would not take advice with respect to the development of gasoline in this country. I believe that some of them have ulterior motives-just as we learned the other day is the case with certain companies in the United States. The rumour is prevalent in several parts of Alberta that oil wells were drilled in times past, discovered to be good producers, and deliberately capped and taken out of production. These rumours are persistent. I do not know whether there is
any truth in them. Obviously, no member of this house has time to investigate. The minister	himself	has	not time.	Would	itnot help matters if he were to insist that every company which has drilled for oil in Alberta or any other part of Canada should produce a detailed account of every drilling it has made and what was done as a result- to make sure that there has been no sabotage? I have heard, from men whom I would not dare to	doubt,	that	wells are	deliberately
kept out of production.
There is another matter which gives me some concern. Is the minister afraid that if gasoline were produced from Athabaska tar sands, it would cost a few cents more than we are now	paying	for	gasoline?	Let it	beclearly understood that if we lose this war, we shall never have any further anxiety about the cost	of gasoline	in the Athabaska	tar
sands. The issue to-day is one of winning the war or losing it; the result might easily be determined by the quantity of gasoline we did or did not produce in any one year, and that year might be the one upon which we are entering at the present time.
Has the minister at his disposal all the money he needs? Is he restricted in any respect? If I could be completely satisfied on that score, my mind would be more at rest. Why worry about the cost of the gasoline? Let us ask this question: if one Adolf Hitler had control of the Athabaska tar sands, does anyone believe for a split second that he would be worrying about the cost of producing the gasoline? How much is Hitler paying in the effort to get through to the Caucasus? What does anybody imagine will be the cost of the gasoline when he gets there? Cost is not entering into his consideration ; what he wants is to get the gasoline; and that, Mr. Chairman, is what we must have, too.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I had been discussing briefly the question of mobilizing our fuel resources in Canada, and I had expressed serious doubt whether any really earnest measures were being taken to meet the danger of a shortage of fuel. I consider that this government's neglect of our fuel supply is altogether reprehensible. I do not believe that any government can possibly be excused before the people to-day or before future generations for neglecting the fuel interests of this
2564
War Appropriation-Supplies

dominion, and I say that for three main reasons, the first being that we have gone mechanical. All over the land, especially in the four western provinces, practically every farmer has gone into mechanized equipment, which means he has probably traded his horses for a car; he has bought an interest in a combine; he is depending on gasoline engines; he has disposed of his pasture. The result is that he has gone into mechanized equipment in such a way that it is impossible for him to get back into a position where he can use horses. This has put our whole economy, particularly agriculture, on a precarious basis; and under such circumstances, to neglect to provide for an adequate fuel supply in Canada is not only a blunder but comes near to being a betrayal.
I maintain that our fuel supply has been neglected. Especially am I led to suspect this by reason of the fact that we have almost entirely neglected alcohol. Alcohol can be made successfully from potatoes. Have we had any potato-made alcohol? Have we had any plants established for the production of alcohol from potatoes? Has there been any programme for the growing of potatoes for that purpose? None that I have heard of, notwithstanding the fact that Canada, from coast to coast, is eminently adapted for the production of potatoes. Then, in regard to wheat, I am informed that good alcohol can be made from this grain. We have had a good deal of talking about making alcohol from wheat; but talk is as far as it has gone, and now the farmers of. the maritimes are limited beyond endurance in the matter of gasoline, while in the west we are getting far less gasoline than we need. Still, only talk. Alcohol can be produced from beet sugar molasses.
Does the hon. member not think it would be a waste of wheat to make alcohol from it?

We might have a billion bushels of wheat in,this country and yet, if we ran out of alcohol, we might be beaten by Hitler. What does the hon. member think about that? It would then have paid us to turn 400 or 500 million bushels more of wheat into alcohol. Bear in mind that we are fighting for our very existence, and when wre are fighting for our existence we must have alcohol fuel., I do not see why so many hon. members seem to do their thinking all in one compartment. They do not think over the whole field. They simply do not realize that we are in danger of being defeated because we lack alcohol or; because we lack gasoline. Sugar beets, will produce alcohol, and the molasses from: such beets can be used to advantage. Have we seen any evidence of a desire to
fMr. Blackmore.]
increase our beet sugar production so as to allow for the possibility of producing alcohol from molasses secured from beet sugar? No evidence at all. All these things serve to indicate that the government must be asleep as far as alcohol and gasoline are concerned. Either that, or it must be under the influence of someone or another who has an ulterior motive. I hope I am wrong, but the evidence seems to indicate that I am only too right.
I wish to turn now for a few moments to another aspect of the question. I am worried about the controllers we have. I know only one or two of these gentlemen; in fact, I hardly know any of them. I do know, however, that the set-up we have under these controllers, twelve of them, each possessing almost absolute power over the particular industry over which he has been placed, is in a position to do this country irreparable harm. Take lumber control. I know nothing about the lumber controller; I have never met him though I think I know his name. But I have heard that prices have been set on lumber at such a figure that many mills that could produce lumber and would do so have been caused to go out of business; prices were fixed at such a level as would enable certain types of mill to succeed but would squeeze out certain other types. If there has been a deliberate design on the part of the lumber controller to accomplish that end, then I say that man has been very unkind to Canada. If lumber mills have been squeezed out of existence at the very time when we need lumber in Canada, and then if, after the lumber controller has destroyed a good deal of the productive power of Canada in connection with lumber, we turn round and say that there is not sufficient lumber to build the houses the people want to build, obviously we have been thrown into a position so false as to appear grotesque.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have kept prices down so that people can build houses. I know of no mill in Canada that is closed. If my hon. friend1 knows of one, I wish he would let me know. To the best of my knowledge the mills are working full out, with a market in the United States for any surplus at better prices than in Canada. I would say that the lumber situation is in a very satisfactory condition at the moment.

I am glad to have
the minister tell us that. One reason why I am saying this is to give him a chance to deny. But from remarks I have heard-and I have definite information from two or three men who, I am sure, knew-there are mills

War Appropriation-Supplies
in British Columbia and certain parts of Alberta that were closed during the past winter because prices were too low.
May I pause here for a moment on the question of price. The minister says that we have kept prices of lumber down in Canada so that people can buy the lumber. That is a most laudable object, entirely commendable. But we can render lumber available to the people of Canada at a low rate without keeping the price to the producer down. That is a fact which is yet to be learned by a considerable number of hon. gentlemen who sit on the government benches. They do not seem to realize that it is possible to do what I am told is done in England, for example with respect to eggs. The producer can be paid 75 cents a dozen for eggs, and the, eggs be sold to the consumer at 50 cents a dozen. The government absorbs the 25 cents. The application of that principle is coming; it must come. It will seem strange to people trained entirely in orthodox thinking, but one of the greatest dangers that confront us to-day is the orthodox thinking which prevails everywhere. If we insist on managing our affairs according to orthodox thinking, and our enemies and competitors follow another kind of thinking, they get ahead of us.
With respect to lumber, there is no reason why the price cannot be made sufficiently remunerative to enable every lumber producer in Canada to produce to the full and yet the lumber be sold at a low rate to the consumer. I use lumber merely as an illustration to show that the set-up is exceedingly dangerous to private industry and may result in so much destruction of our production as will subject us to the danger of inflation because of a shortage of goods. This is a result of the system of controls that we have. I am not sure that any controller is abusing his power, but I would feel very much safer if there were a system of supervising controllers so that we could be sure that no controller is taking advantage of his position to help his friends at the expense of other producers.
I turn now to another matter which is causing a good deal of difficulty in my constituency and other parts of western Canada. There have been restrictions in regard to automobiles. We have been told that we can have only so many tires; that only so much gasoline is available; that no new cars are being produced; the result is that many people who have come to depend entirely on cars for transportation are at their wit's end to know what to do.
I call this to the attention of the minister in case he has not noticed it. Twenty years ago before the coming of the automobile
every farmer had his buggy- and his wagon. There were plenty of buggies, plenty of wagons, in the stores of the implement dealers. There are now no wagons on many farms. In many instances there are no buggies on the farms. There are no wagons or buggies to speak of in the hands of the dealers; men do not know where they are going to buy wagons and buggies. I wonder whether provision has been made for the manufacture of wagons and buggies to take the place of the automobiles.
This is a most serious situation. It is difficult to get harness; it is difficult to get horse-drawn machinery, where men- have gone in for ploughs that require a tractor, not to mention the difficulty of getting horses. When men have put all their working capital into automotive equipment and machinery they have no capital with which to buy horses and horse-drawn vehicles. The result is that farmers in many parts of Canada are faced with a situation which to them appears utterly impossible. I -wonder whether the minister is taking precautions to see that that situation is met.
These are some real difficulties which I have presented to the minister. I think it would relieve us if he could tell us that all is well.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We are taking special precautions to try to give the farmers the tires they need to carry on business. As far as the gasoline situation in the prairie provinces is concerned, we are fairly secure because we have a local source of supply partly in Alberta and partly in the neighbouring states.
Is anything being done regarding the manufacture of alcohol from potatoes or wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have an ample source of alcohol so far. All the distilleries in the east and in the west have been turned fairly well to the production of alcohol. We can step up our production of alcohol as much as is needed for any ordinary purposes.
Has the minister any means for supervising the work of the controllers so as to make sure that they are not abusing their powers?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; the chairman of the control board has a staff for that purpose, and of course the deputy minister and I exercise authority over the board. No order can be issued without my examination, approval and signature.

Has the minister any means whereby a man might be able to send in a complaint? Suppose a lumberman finds
War Appropriation-Supplies

prices are being set in such a way as to discriminate against him; is there provision whereby he can write in and complain without endangering himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: He can, and does very frequently. We get plenty of complaints.

The other day when the minister was before the committee he informed us that since the commencement of the war he had awarded contracts totalling over $4,000,000,000. I envy him his ability to discuss in this house, with very few references to his notes, such a wide variety of expenditures. I might remind the committee that total expenditures in connection with the last war, together with disbursements in connection with demobilization, amounted to $1,695,000,000, or only a fraction of the amount handled by the minister's department. If we add all expenditures chargeable to the consolidated fund, chargeable to capital, all railway subsidies, all other charges and the cost of war demobilization from confederation up to 1935, the total will be less than three times the amount of money being spent by this one department.
It is physically impossible for members of this house to follow intelligently all the expenditures of this large department, but this evening I wish to discuss one company which is under the supervision of the minister, and which, in my opinion, has not received sufficient consideration here. I refer to Wartime Housing, Limited. Unfortunately, at the commencement of the present war Canada was in a very bad way as far as housing our people was concerned. At the commencement of the last war we had, in most cities, vacancies of from 7 to 15 per cent of the total, while at the commencement of the present war less than one house out of every one hundred was vacant in most of our cities. Unfortunately, during the years prior to the outbreak of the war the cities of Canada did not carry out regular, thorough surveys to ascertain the exact condition of housing within their limits. I have a report coming from the city of Halifax and issued in 1932 in which are set forth the conditions prevailing there. From the investigation made it would appear that 11,197 men, women and children were living under conditions believed to be serious enough to be included in a special survey. The most recent survey available from Montreal is one which was published in 1935, which admits that
18,000	persons in that city need rehousing, and that a total of 70,000 dwellings were required at rentals below the levels which private industry could afford. An excellent report was prepared on conditions in Toronto when the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. 
Bruce) was lieutenant-governor of Ontario. According to that report, not only were bad housing conditions discovered but the presence of a serious housing shortage was also detected. The report goes on to say:
A surplus of households is at present absorbed by doubling up and overcrowding. If reasonably full employment were to return, and marriages delayed by depression were to take place, it is probable that a shortage of some
25,000	dwelling units would become apparent.
The most comprehensive report available comes from the city of Winnipeg, where they have been so fortunate as to have a public health department which each year conducts a very thorough investigation and submits a full report. In the most recent report we find that they have reached an all-time low in the number of vacancies, which means that more and more families are having to crowd together. The report goes on:
This condition is, of course, in conflict with our health and other by-laws, but it is evident that there is little we can do about it.
And further on:
During the past five years, the total dwellings and suites provided was 1,886, while during the same period, there were 18,322 marriages-one dwelling or suite for approximately every ten marriages. Of course many of the marriages are of people from outside the city, but if three-fourths of the marriages were of city people, the rate would be only one dwelling or suite provided for approximately every seven marriages.
I believe hon. members will understand what a serious problem is presented by these figures. Since this report was made, a great many of the young men who have joined the forces have married. These young men are risking their lives to fight for their homes; yet on coming back to Canada many of them find that we have not homes available for them. Their families find it impossible to secure housing in many of our larger cities within the price range they can afford. The report concerning Winnipeg goes on to say:
Surely our present housing shortage cannot continue much longer. The risk to health of our substandard housing, not to mention that of the fire hazard in our nondescript tenements, may be brought home to us with painful remorse.
This report gives an idea of how costly it is to maintain these large slum areas in our cities. A few years ago a survey was carried out in Winnipeg, for the purpose of which they divided the city into three areas, numbered one, two and three. Areas one and two included the worst slum districts, while area three included the rest of the city. The report indicates that the arrests per thousand of population in area No. 1 was 21T; in area No. 2, 52-2, and in the rest of the city, 6-5.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Cases handled by the children's bureau per thousand of population in area No. 1 was 9*1; in area No. 2, 9-2, and in the rest of the city, 4-2. Juvenile court cases per thousand of population, in area No. 1, 16-9; in area No. 2, 23-7, and in area No. 3, 11-5. St. Boniface out-patients per thousand of population: in area No. 1, 22-9; in area No. 2, 34-2, and in area No. 3, 5-3. Hospital public ward admissions per thousand of population: in area No. 1, 91-1; in area No. 2, 101-4, and in area No. 3, 52-9. Scarlet fever and diphtheria: in area No. 1, 13-6; in area No. 2, 15-7, and in area No. 3, 7-5.
This report gives the comparative cost to the city of social services in the two special areas compared with the rest of the city, indicating that in terms of dollars and cents it is an expensive business to allow these large slum areas to exist. The report goes on to say that with regard to seven essential services the cost to the city in the two special areas was $639,000, while the cost for the rest of the city was $612,000; but if the cost for these slum areas had been at the same per capita rate as for the rest of the city, that cost would have been $189,000. In other words, there was a yearly cost in areas Nos. 1 and 2 of $450,000 in excess of the cost for the rest of the city, which means that it cost the people of that attractive city nearly half a million dollars yearly to maintain this large slum area. It was estimated that if a million dollars had been spent in slum clearance, it would have been possible to amortize this amount over a twenty-year period at an annual cost of $77,000, which would give the city a saving of about $350,000 a year.
I might direct attention to an interesting report that was presented to this house in 1935, when a special committee was set up to look into the housing situation. I am sorry to say that only three of the members of that committee are still here: the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church); the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray), and the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden). In this report there is a statement showing the cost of the slums in the city of Cleveland:
According to an intensive survey made in Cleveland of a slum district where two and one half per cent of the population lived, 22 per cent of the murders were committed, 6-8 per cent of boy delinquency, and 12J per cent of the tuberculosis deaths occurred in this area. Although the per capita cost of fire protection in the city of Cleveland is only $3.12 the cost in the slum area is $18.72. Although the total tax income of this area is only $225,000 the total municipal expenses are $1,356,000, leaving a deficit of $1,131,000, which must be made up by the rest of the community. If you add the contribution
of the various unofficial agencies, such as visiting nurses association, maternity hospitals, etc., we add $615,000, so the total deficiency is $1,740,000.
In the same report a table is submitted showing what proportion of the family income should be spent in rent. White-collar workers, receiving an income of from $1,000 to $1,500, might spend one-third of the income for rent, or $34.70 a month. Artisans, receiving an income of $850 to $1,025, spent one-quarter or $19.60 a month. Semi-skilled workers could not spend over one-fifth, or $12.50 a month on the average, and unskilled, on the wages they were receiving, could not spend more than $9.20 a month. The committee submitted recommendations which have received consideration by subsequent governments, but unfortunately the recommendations have not been acted upon to as great an extent as might have been expected. In the evidence it is emphasized that:
A national emergency will soon develop unless the building of dwellings be greatly increased.
The formulation, institution and pursuit of a policy of adequate housing should be accepted as a social responsibility.
There is no apparent prospect of the low rental housing need being met through unaided private enterprise, building for profit.
This report was submitted in 1935. Unfortunately since that time very little consideration has been given to achieving this general objective. I am very glad to say that the government has recognized that the housing of people in our industries is an essential part of our war effort. In the United States the same policy is being followed.
I have in my hands a copy of Business Week for January 3, 1942, in which it is stated that the President of the United States in the previous week had signed an appropriation to bring housing money up over the billion mark. It mentions that defence housing has gained recognition as a major war project. During the last war United States industry found that they had wastages of as much as 10 per cent, as a direct result of being unable to find for their workers housing adjacent to factories. We are already experiencing similar difficulties in Canada.
Recently I visited one of the munitions industries in the Toronto region. The people of Canada have invested over $5,000,000 in providing plant and equipment in this particular factory, and I must congratulate the minister upon the excellent work that ha3 been done there. As far as I could see they are doing a very good job, but the management informed me that they are now experiencing a problem which apparently had not been anticipated. There are men who are coming as far as fifteen miles to work. During a
War Appropriation-Supplies

time of unemployment men will travel fifteen or twenty miles, if necessary, to find employment ; but during a time of nearly full employment, if a man can find work within three blocks of his home, even if it is in a nonessential industry, he is likely to find an excuse for being dismissed from the essential industry. I am informed that this particular company has submitted a brief to the department suggesting that consideration be given to the providing of houses in that particular area.
A little over a year ago the minister persuaded the government to agree to set aside
810.000,000 for the purpose of going into the business of building houses. Since that time I understand commitments have been undertaken which will require at least $30,000,000. I am not criticizing the minister for the amount of money that is being spent. As a matter of fact I do not think he is spending enough money on this particular phase of the war effort. If we assume that it is going to cost a billion dollars a year to produce the munitions, it is conceivable that we shall have a wastage of 5 per cent or even 10 per cent. We suffer a loss of $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 a year as a direct result of not having adequate housing available in the areas the men are employed. Therefore I am not criticizing the minister for spending too much money on this very important project.
I do feel, however, that the projects are open to criticism, on two grounds. In the first place we are building potential slum areas under Wartime Housing, Limited. I know the minister has stated that these houses are to be demolished when the war is over. Past experiences in every country however, have demonstrated that temporary houses will not be torn down as long as there are in the various communities less desirable houses being occupied. If the moneys spent on wartime housing were being spent in isolated places where industries have been established-industries which will be demolished when the war is over-I would not be so concerned. But if we look over the returns which have been brought down to the house, we find that large sums of money have been spent in Halifax, Hamilton, Vancouver and other cities in Canada where there is a very serious shortage of permanent housing.
Therefore, in deciding a policy of wartime housing the government should consider first of all the amount of labour available in Canada, the amount of material available, and the time element-whether there is an immediate hurry to have these houses built. As far as cost is concerned, the pronouncement

by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Defence should be the policy of the government, namely, that whatever is physically possible will be made financially possible. That being so, if it is physically possible to build permanent houses, then by all means let us make it financially possible. We cannot afford in Canada at this time to spend $30,000,000 on the building of potential slum areas. I submit that the temporary houses which are being built are going to become potential slum areas.
I feel the department is open to a second criticism, on cost and on construction. Hon. members have been invited by the minister to visit houses in Hull built by Wartime Housing, Limited. Some lion, members have accepted his invitation, and I think all who have made the visit will agree with me that the taxpayers of Canada have paid a great deal of money for flimsily constructed houses. A return brought down recently placed the cost of these houses at $3,379.
In Ottawa within the last year permanent houses have been built by the national housing administration, under the Department of Finance. I urge hon. members who are interested in housing to visit the wartime housing buildings in Hull, and then to visit the national housing administration houses in Ottawa. A return was brought down on March 27 giving information respecting the building done by the national housing administration. My first question was: "How many single housing units were built under the supervision of the national housing administration during the period September, 1939, to December, 1941?" The answer was "12,852 units." That is a valuable contribution toward solving our housing problem. It is not yet enough, but it is over 12,000 more than we might have had. Then I asked as to the average cost per house, and it was shown that the average cost was $3,750. My next question was as to how many low-priced houses had been built by the national housing administration at $2,500 each, and the answer was "2,433."
I have some plans before me showing the type of houses built under the national housing administration. I refer particularly to a house twenty-four feet by twenty-four feet with two bedrooms, a good sized living room, an attractive kitchen with built-in cupboards and so on and two windows, and a bathroom. This is a permanent house with a full-sized basement, containing a furnace. I recently visited one of these homes in Ottawa, and I was advised by the owner that this house was secure by his making a cash payment of $250 and monthly payments of about $20

War Appropriation-Supplies
including interest, principal and taxes, over a twenty-year period. Actually these people are getting a house of this kind for $250, because their monthly payments are no greater than the rent which wTould be asked for a similar house. They are paying $16.35 a month for twenty years to retire principal and pay the interest, and the taxes bring up the payments to around $20. Recently a change has been made requiring the amount borrowed under the national housing scheme to be repaid within a fifteen-year period. Under this plan, during the first five years when only small expenditures would be required for repairs, the payment amounts to $19.62, and for the next ten years payments drop to $14.60.
The point I am trying to make is that people who are living in these homes are home owners. They take pride in their flowers, trees and lawn; they take pride in owning their first home, and that is a very important consideration. In the basement of this particular home a ping-pong table had been in use during the winter months. This was a fine place for them to spend their evenings. In contrast to this, we have the type of house erected in Hull, built of inferior materials, without a basement or furnace, erected by Wartime Housing Limited. Strange as it may seem, people in Hull are paying $30.20 a month for a house that they will never own, a house that will never give them the source of pride which they would otherwise have.
Speaking in the house last November the minister made reference to having met someone who was living in one of these wartime houses who would not exchange it for a brick-veneer house built some years ago at a cost of $5,200. I do not, for a moment, doubt the minister's word, but he did not mention where that man lived. I think he must have lived up in the territory represented by the hon. member for Yukon. I cannot conceive of a person in Hull or Welland or Hamilton being willing to exchange a $5,200 brick-veneer house for a house built by wartime housing. I can conceive of a man who had built a house in Hudson Bay junction, where I lived for ten years, or in the Yukon or Churchill or the Pas, and who found that he was compelled to live in another province, being willing to trade a $5,200 house for a house of that sort. But I cannot understand anyone being willing to exchange a house that had cost $5,200 for any house built by wartime housing in the same area.
Recently I received from Vancouver an illustrated booklet showing three houses which had been built there under the national housing administration scheme. These houses are quite attractive looking, nicely painted, with brick
chimneys, lined flues, full-sized basements, furnaces, hardwood floors and modern conveniences. They were built at a cost of $2,500 each. In the same booklet there is a picture of houses built by wartime housing. When the booklet was prepared it was assumed that these houses were being built at a cost of around $2,000, but the return I have states that these temporary houses, without basements and without furnaces, were built at a cost of $2,996.97. I cannot understand how permanent houses can be built in greater Vancouver for a down payment of $250 cash and $20 a month for a twenty-year period, when other workers are required to pay from $20 to $30 a month for inferior houses which will never become their property.
There is one other point I want to make before I conclude. So far the government has not given consideration to the building of houses which will be available for the families of men who are with the navy, the army or the air force. From what has been said in the house, I gather that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) does not consider that the building of houses is his concern. I find that on April 28, as reported on page 1942 of Hansard, he stated what unfortunately appears to be the position of the government. He said:
I must take this position-it is the position taken by my colleague the Minister of Finance *-that this question of housing the citizens of Canada-not people moving transiently-is the problem of the municipalities rather than that of the federal government.
As I mentioned earlier, hundreds of men from every part of Canada have joined the air force, the navy and the army, prepared to go any place in the world and to risk their lives. The relatives of some of these men are coming to our civic authorities and saying that their husbands are away fighting for their homes, but they have no homes; they complain that they cannot secure houses. The wife of a private with two children receives a monthly allowance of $79. I should like to know where in Ottawa or Toronto or Hamilton or Winnipeg the wife of a soldier would be able to rent suitable quarters for one-fifth of that amount, or $15.80.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply is in charge of the building programme for the government, and I think he should give careful consideration to the building of low-priced houses to be made available to the relatives of those who are with our forces. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think I have explained this several times, but I shall be glad to go over the ground once more. The national housing policy presents quite a different problem from that presented by wartime housing. The money for national housing is available and has been continuously available to anyone who cares to take advantage of it. It has been used largely by speculative builders who took advantage of the terms quite legitimately in order to build houses, and sell them on a rental basis.
Where has that sort of thing been done?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The town of Port Arthur is one place about which I happen to know something.

They are built by
speculative builders?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
They are sold on a rental-lease basis. The owner is seldom the initial borrower. Frequently he is, but I think the majority of these houses are built on a speculative arrangement.
{Mr. Nicholson.]
I think the minister is misinformed in that connection. As I understand the act, the owner must be the borrower.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Well, we will not argue that; my hon. friend may be better posted than I am. But I know that in my own town the arrangements at least are made as a rule by a builder, perhaps for an owner, and the owner may be brought into it before the house is started. Usually these houses are built, not singly, but a number at the same time, in my own town.
I believe the mortgage is made by the owner direct with the department; I am not sure of the mechanics of the thing. This arrangement is, of course, for a house built by a man who lives in a community in which he expects to remain for many years. Wartime housing is not for that sort of an owner. As my hon. friend knows, we have moved great numbers of our population from one city to another, from the prairies to the cities, from the cities to plants built in small communities; and wartime housing is built to take care of the man who has been so dislocated. That is all that it was ever intended for. It is quite different and distinct from houses built under the National Housing Act.
For this purpose we have provided a type of construction which, while giving the owner every comfort, is not expensive. My hon. friend speaks of "inferior materials". He is quite mistaken. The housing materials which go into the wartime housing project are the best that are used in building generally. They are not elaborate, but there is nothing shoddy about the wartime housing house.
Has the minister seen the houses in Hull?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The houses in Hull are like those elsewhere. Has my hon. friend seen a wartime housing development which has been in existence for a year or two? I went to Windsor yesterday and saw wartime houses there. I found that there was a wartime housing improvement association of tenants putting in shrubs and building playgrounds. I may say, as one who has something to do with this, that I felt quite proud of that community. I have yet to hear a complaint from a tenant. I visit these housing projects wherever I can, and I have heard plenty of criticisms from dealers in lumber, from dealers in hardware, and from people like my hon. friend, but I have yet to hear a complaint from a tenant; in fact some very nice remarks have been made by tenants of these houses. It is always a pleasure for me to visit them.
My hon. friend asks why they cost-as he says-more than permanent housing. I doubt

War Appropriation-Supplies
very much if they do. But I would point this out. The builder of a home under the National Housing Act becomes a permanent citizen of his community and he is entitled to the rights of a citizen. He goes on a street which is developed; he attaches to the existing sewerage system and the existing water mains. The city pays part of his local improvements and he pays the remainder in taxes over a period of years. He is a taxpayer; he is entitled to the use of the services of the city, to everything which is the right and privilege of the taxpayer. But wartime housing is a temporary invader of the community. It does not become a citizen; it does not pay ordinary taxes, but it relieves the city of any expenditure on its account. When we go into a city we very often build our own streets, our own sewerage systems, our own water systems. Sometimes the expenditures for these purposes are very considerable. There is a case in Hamilton, I believe, where we have built almost a complete sewerage system and a complete water system. All that is charged against the houses. Our tenants do not pay taxes. We, as owners, pay the city the school taxes, and something more, by an arrangement we have made in all the provinces and which has been approved by the provincial governments and accepted by the cities in which we build. Therefore the tenants of our houses pay their rents, but no taxes.
As to the reason why these houses are constructed as they are. We do not wish to establish populations permanently where they are to-day. It is not desirable. The city of Windsor, I suppose, has almost twice the population it had at the beginning of the war. These people came from farms; they have houses elsewhere; we hope that after the war a goodly number will go back to their farms; that is, to their permanent residences. We have built sizeable communities around war plants which we know definitely will close down after the war-for instance, plants manufacturing ammunition and plants filling shells. These are temporary war projects and must necessarily be sold. There is no post-war use, that I know of, of an ammunition plant or a shell-filling plant. We had them during the last war, and when it was over the buildings were torn down. I doubt whether these plants will be demolished, but they cannot, I believe, be adapted to any other useful purpose. This means that these communities will disappear after the war. The advantage of the present method of construction is that the tenants can take these houses with them if they like. They are easily demountable, easily removable. They can be put upon
permanent foundations, and first-class houses can be had with a very small additional expenditure. We hope that by building this class of house we can, after the war, if there is a movement of population elsewhere, take care of them. We have not a number of houses which, my hon. friend says, are bound to grow into slums. Nothing of the sort. If there is any tendency of that sort, the houses will be removed. In case the houses are needed where they are to-day, it is the simplest thing in the world to jack them up, put a permanent basement under them, install a central heating system, and thereby have as good a house of that class as can be obtained.
The type of house which we use is the type which is being used to the south of us for the same purpose. Demountable houses are being constructed there. Inquiries lead us to believe that the housing situation in the United States is not being met in as orderly a way as it is in Canada. We have been able to keep up to reasonable requirements, and we intend to continue doing so.
We do not lead the way in housing. We like to have a demand before we build, but we are reasonably keeping up with the demand. Officials of wartime housing are constantly studying the various centres of war industry to determine the housing needs. We have local committees who also study the question. If we have a considerable number of applications for wartime housing, there is no delay in starting a new project. In Windsor there are now, I believe, 1,300 houses. In addition, there are about 700 applications, and we are starting immediately to build another 500 houses in that city.
Therefore we are keeping reasonably up to the requirements of our war industries. As far as the ordinary civilian population is concerned, that is a somewhat different story. It is not the purpose of wartime housing to look after them. We still have the National Housing Act which can be used, and if, as my hon. friend says, it is so much better and cheaper, it is surprising that more people do not take advantage of it. In any event, we have the National Housing Act. We have helped out on occasions in many cities. If there is a demand of the type to which my hon. friend refers, we make available to the city, by arrangement, a certain number of war-time houses. I believe that in Hamilton we have made twenty available. Usually five or ten are all that are required. Windsor is exceptional. There, in addition to the twenty I have mentioned, we intend to make a few more available.
War Appropriation-Supplies

I assure my hon. friend that, where there is wartime housing, no conditions are allowed to rise which the city itself considers to be a condition of distress. We have always been quite willing to help a city in circumstances of that kind. I think wartime housing has served a useful purpose, and I am not at all ashamed of the type of houses we have built. As temporary houses go, I think they are first rate. We have a list of satisfied tenants, and I have yet to hear a direct complaint from one of them. The houses are well looked after by local committees, and on the whole I must say that the enterprise has turned out quite as well as I hoped it would when the work was first planned.

The minister has not fully dealt with the question regarding the cost in Hull. The sum of $3,379 appears to me ts be a very high cost. I agree that in areas where the population will not be located permanently there is a real place for wartime housing, but these houses in Hull will be occupied, for example, by people employed in the Ottawa Car and Aircraft, and the situation here is that we need permanent houses, and a great many of them. If the time factor were of importance I could understand that some of these houses might be built, but in the return brought down the other day it was shown, with regard to the houses in Hull, that they were supposed to 'be completed, some by October 17 and all by December 17. I was there the other day and only thirty-four or thirty-six were occupied by the 1st of May, which would indicate that there has not been a very great demand for houses immediately for the people considered to be in war industry. These houses cost $3,379, and I submit that in Ottawa better houses have been built for $2,500. It is true that these minimum cost houses have only two bedrooms while the others have four, but how is the difference in cost to be explained? There are lots available in Ottawa where houses could be built, where it would not be necessary to go to the expense of providing the services that are furnished in Hull. Taking into consideration the needs of the community in Ottawa and Hull, I cannot see why the people of Canada should embark upon a programme of building houses, paying $3,379 for temporary houses, when better permanent houses might have been built for the same sum or less.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The proper place to investigate the cost of housing is in the committee on war expenditures, where all costs are laid on the table and one can see where the money goes. It is no use arguing with me that this is an expensive house when I say it is a cheap house. I know what materials cost. I know what labour costs. I know what sewage and land cost. I know the houses are well built, built by an expert builder, and at reasonable cost. My hon. friend can debate all night that the houses are expensive, but if we lay the costs on the table it will be necessary for him ;o show where the money was wasted. I love to hear people who have no possible way of knowing anything about the building business, in this case, two gentlemen of the Gospel, which is a fine pursuit, arguing with me, who have been all my life in such business and know something about the facts, and telling me that these houses are too expensive. It is hardly an even argument, and we could go on arguing for some time.

The minister mentioned the committee on war expenditures. That raises a very important question. Let me point out to him that the war expenditures committee has been selected, and when it was set up the Prime Minister said that it could be enlarged. Three subcommittees were set up. I have a few words to say in connection with this housing proposition. This was a Conservative policy in 1935 at a time when hon. gentlemen of the third party did nothing about it. During the dark days of the depression in 1935 when the Bennett government was in office a motion on the subject of housing and reconstruction was made by me when the construction industry was down and out. The resolution was debated for two days; a housing committee was appointed by our then leader, and after sitting for three months it presented a comprehensive report to the house. Under this resolution wartime housing only is before the committee at the present time.	I am not going to discuss
housing except to say that during the last war I had a great deal to do with the housing situation in Toronto and the many suburbs and municipalities clustered around that city with a population of 1,100,000 people. The city took over the street railway radials and started the buses, because the housing problem is largely a transportation problem, and provided good municipal services, water, roads, sewers, and other services. If you have the transportation and the sewers, water supplies, lights and heating, then the housing will go ahead. Twice the number of houses were built at that time than in the years after the war, and shortly before its close by the city building civic car lines.

So I urge upon the government a vast shipbuilding scheme, and not an hour or a day should be lost. We are not yet able and will not for a year yet be able to challenge the supremacy of Japan in the Pacific. Japan now has the same command over the Pacific that Germany has over the Baltic when the Russian ports are closed by ice, and in the Black sea. Japan does not need to establish a military blockade of the main forces of her enemies to keep them away from the areas she has seized so far. She is able to hold them without that. She is there in sea command. Japan is pursuing her campaign in an area stretching over fifteen thousand miles, going from island to island like a circus, but this cannot go on forever. I believe once she loses command of the sea she cannot supply or reinforce her scattered garrisons or draw from the conquered territories those supplies for which she entered the war. There is only one road to victory for the allies; that is, to reestablish command of the Pacific, as effectively as we now have command of the Atlantic. I suggest that there might be some reorganization of the work in the production department. Indeed, I have some suggestions. Would it not be well to arrange now to establish regional executive production councils in the provinces, who could decentralize this work of production. They could meet weekly in regional centres and thereby ensure administrative decentralization, acceleration of decisions and economy of money and man-power. Supply departments and all appropriate government services would be represented. speechtext: In connection with shipbuilding I might give the committee some information which would be of interest. Tonight at midnight two west coast yards are each launching a 10,000-ton freighter.
