There is a 10-inch cement block wall. Theijgtfs a pipe furnace complete, valued at $165:' The plumbing was of a superior kind, and the joints were hidden in the floor as they should be. They were not exposed, as they were in wartime housing building. There was a cement laundry-tub, a hot-water tank and a coil. There was a built-in bathtub, with shower. The wiring was complete, with double switches, centre lights, a nice fireplace in the living room, and a good chimney. There were double floors done in oak, and inlaid linoleum on the kitchen and bathroom floors. The outside was of rug brick and asphalt shingles. There was a cement walk and an outer porch. It was graded, and a lawn had been sown.
I asked a number of people to compare the values, and one said that he would rather pay $3,500 for the house built under national housing than $800 for the house built by wartime housing. I have great respect for the minister's knowledge of construction. The construction company he headed has a reputation throughout Canada, but I think he is mistaken when he states that the houses built by wartime housing are built so that they can be taken 
down and the people can take them with them. He says that everything is demountable in sections, but perhaps I may be permitted to give my opinion. I cannot see how one would be able to take asphalt shingles off these houses. The floors are laid across the different sections, and they could not be removed. The salvage value of what would be left would not be very much.
This lumberman told me that the salvage value would be about $400. That is what he would bid if he were figuring on buying. I do not see how it can be said that they are demountable in sections when one would have to take up the floor, tear out the gyproc and take off the asphalt shingles. As I say, this lumberman estimated the value of the lumber in the house at about $400. If the price of these buildings is anything like the price of the rest of the houses-I have a question on the order paper to-morrow asking for the cost of these houses

I think it is time that the matter was investigated.
Probably the real explanation was given by the Minister of Labour who, I think, settled the matter when he said, first, that he had not lived in a house as good as these when he was first married. That has no bearing on what it is costing the people of Canada to put up these houses. Second, he said that he was a personal friend of the president who, I believe, is Mr. Pigott, a dollar-a-year man, and of the .general manager, Mr. Goggin, who is receiving $10,000 a year as head of wartime housing. This wartime housing is a government company with the central managing point in Toronto, and it lets contracts to various contractors. I think the Minister of Labour put his finger upon the point when he said, third, that the main thing to look forward to at this time was that the construction industry should have a cushion after the war. I think it is far more important that the people should see that this administration gives value for the money expended. We should not be providing soft cushions for any industry at the expense of people living in homes like these.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think when my hon. friend said that he went through the houses with a lumber dealer he told the whole story. Naturally the lumber dealers are not fond of wartime housing because all the lumber is bought wholesale in carload lots.
That should make it cheaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It makes it so much cheaper that the local lumber dealers can not handle it.

War Appropriation-Supplies
There was no competition. This man was an independent man; he was not interested in contracts, and he was not going there with that idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend said that he was a lumber dealer. I suppose he will not change his mind on that?
I am not changing my mind on anything I have said.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We will settle that he was a local lumber dealer.
I said that he was an experienced lumberman.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Not a lumber dealer? Surely my hon. friend should know whether he was a lumber dealer. He said he was a lumberman. What does a lumberman do? Does he deal in lumber?

He understands lumber.
Mr. H0W7E: Does he deal in lumber? Can my hon. friend say yes or no?

Yes; he deals in
lumber.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: All right, thank you. The construction of these houses are let by competitive tender. Every reputable contractor in the countiy has a chance to bid, and the contract is given to the low bidder. The materials are bought in carload lots at controlled prices. If my hon. friend cares to sit in on the committee on wartime expenditures he will find that the prices will be laid on the table. He will then see, that they are very attractive prices indeed for materials. As I say, the materials are bought in carload lots with every discount that the trade can possibly stand. My hon. friend complains that his group is not allowed to attend this committee, but I have a note here which says-
The minister should not put words in my mouth and say that we were not allowed to attend the committee. I said that we had no representative on the subcommittee investigating wartime housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I understand that you are allowed to attend and take part in the deliberations, and I am told that when hon. members found that it was not a public meeting, they left the subcommittee. That is my information.

I rise to a
question of privilege. The minister ought to get his information from the same expert
authority he has been demanding that other people should get theirs from. He certainly ought not to base remarks made in this house on notes handed to him unless he knows the note has some basis in fact. This group have never left any committee. I should like to point out to the minister that we have only one representative on the wartime expenditures committee, and there are three subcommittees. Consequently we have only a representative on the one subcommittee, No. 3, and we have no representative on subcommittees Nos. 1 and 2. Any hon. member may sit in on the committee, but we have no representation on those two subcommittees.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Nevertheless the first speaker attended the committee.
He is not a member of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: He attended for a while.

He attended one or two meetings, but it was made very clear to him that if he attended any sittings in camera he was bound to secrecy regarding information given there when discussing matters such as the one before this committee now. The point I want to make to the minister is this: He says it is up to the committee on war expenditures to investigate these prices, but our group has no representation on that committee. Despite the promise of the Prime Minister that the membership of that committee would be increased, the supporters of the government, eighteen out of twenty-four, turned down a motion moved by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) to increase the size of that committee so that we might have representation on the subcommittees. The only place where we can get any information in connection with wartime housing is in that committee because we have no representation on the subcommittees investigating the matter. We have never left any committee at any time, nor have we refused to sit on any committee in the discharge of our duties.

I think the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) wants to be fair with the members of this committee and with the members of the committee on war expenditures. That committee was set up on the same basis as all other special committees are set up. I understand that there were eight special committees sitting to-day, and there are eight or nine cooperative Commonwealth Federation members. As hon. members have said time after time, it is simply impossible
War Appropriation-Supplies

to attend all these special committees, the three subcommittees of the war expenditures committee and the sittings of the house.
We will take care of that.

My hon, friend appreciates that. With reference to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), he was invited to sit in. We were glad to have his opinion and he was permitted to ask questions. When the committee decided to sit in camera the hon. member withdrew, as it was his privilege to do. I do not think he felt that he was being treated unfairly by the committee. He had every opportunity of sitting there and listening to the evidence given and the questions asked in connection with this matter now being investigated by that committee. We hope to bring in a report on the matter.
We are entirely out of order in discussing the work of a committee before it has presented its report.
I quite appreciate that, Mr. Chairman, but it is unfortunate that you did not call others to order before now.

I should like to ask the minister about the policy followed to fix the rentals of these wartime houses. I have here a dispatch which appeared in one of the Ottawa papers last month, reading as follows: Replying to aldermen who alleged that rentals of Wartime Housing, Limited's houses in Hull of $30.20 a month are too high, Mayor Brunet said last night the reason was that representations were made to rent them at that figure to wartime housing officials. The representations were made so as to protect Hull property owners.
Are these rents fixed to protect property owners, or are they fixed on a basis of retiring the government investment over a period of five or ten years, or just what policy is followed in deciding that the rent shall be $30.20 a month? I understand the house has four bedrooms.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It is not a four-bedroom
house.

The only houses that are being rented in Hull are, I understand, the four-bedroom houses. The others, I understand, are not yet completed. Anyway, the press report says that the rent is $30.20. What policy is followed in relation to the item which I read?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend is not correct. The standard four-room house is-

It is a six-roomed
house. I said four bedrooms.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The six-room house is rented at $30. Of the four-room houses, what we call the smaller four-room is rented at $22, the larger four-room at $25, and the six-room house at $30. These amounts were fixed1 on the basis of reasonable amortization of the cost, but were lowered somewhat to be in keeping with the average salary paid to the class of tenant that we get. It is somewhat below the amount required for amortization.

When the original
order in council, P.C. 1286, was passed on February 24, 1941, it contained this provision:
Such agreement shall have no effect until it has been approved by the governor general in council; and upon such approval the company may exercise the powers and shall discharge the duties set forth in such agreement; and also may exercise and shall discharge such other powers and duties as may in such order in council, or from time to time be conferred or charged upon it by the governor general in council.
On the 24th of April another order in council was passed adding:
or by the Minister of Munitions and Supply under the authority of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
In other words, when the first order in council was passed it must have been thought desirable to refer these agreements to the governor general in council. Later, that position was reconsidered, and apparently they just refer them to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Why the change in policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
As projects are approved,
each individual project is approved by order in council and the appropriation is made. As a matter of mechanics, the individual contracts are signed by munitions and supply. It is thought unwise first to get the project approved and then go back and get the individual contracts approved. Personally I see nothing sinister in that; if my hon. friend does, perhaps we shall change it back again.

I am merely asking
for information. I think I am entitled to it.
My next question is this. Section 4, paragraph (c) of P.C. 1286, reads:
(c) it may draw upon the personnel and upon the economic and other technical resources relating to housing presently available in the government service, and in particular shall utilize the services of the housing branch of the Department of Finance.
Valuable work has been done in this field by the national housing administration, by the Department of Pensions and National Health, and by the national research council. The research work done over a period of

War Appropriation-Supplies
years could be made available for wartime housing, and particularly they should use the services of the housing branch of the Department of Finance. I find that the later order in council, P.C. 2842, deletes this paragraph. What was the reason for the deletion?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: A considerable part of the staff of the national housing branch was moved in with wartime housing. They seemed somewhat unhappy about the arrangement, and gradually drifted back to Ottawa, and I doubt if any of them are left. But such information as was at hand was supposed to be placed at the disposal of wartime housing, and I daresay it was.

My information was that no advantage had been taken of the work done by the national research council, or by the Department of Pensions and National Health. I know that similar information can be obtained, over a period of time, but it seems to me that the provision in paragraph (c) of section 4 was a valuable one, enabling the company to "draw upon the personnel and upon the economic and other technical resources relating to housing presently available", and I cannot see any good reason why, on the 24th of April, it was decided that they should not take advantage of that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I am sure they have drawn on all the information that could be of any value to them. The question was thoroughly studied. Mr. Somerville, one of the directors, is an architect of wide exeprience, who has always interested himself in housing projects. The other directors are men of considerable experience, and I know that in the course of their work they have consulted not only our own institutions, but various authorities in Washington and elsewhere. I believe that no lack of study has been given to these houses.

Perhaps we can take up another subject for a few minutes. The minister has made statements which would lead one to believe that the government is now thinking of embarking upon a policy of finding oil in Canada. Of course the reason is quite easy to see: there is a great shortage of oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: There is no change of policy.

Could the minister explain in what way the government proposes to carry out that policy? For example, does the minister propose to encourage private
companies to do the exploring for oil and to undertake the research work, or will such companies be subsidized by the government, or is it the intention that the government itself will drill the wells and take whatever other steps are necessary to try to find more oil in Canada? That is one question I should like the minister to answer.
Another is with regard to power. He told the committee last year that it was not the policy of the government to aid in the development of power. In the intervening period, I believe, some assistance has been given to certain power companies in the way of allowances for taxation purposes. I do not know whether that has been done extensively, but I understand that it has been done in some instances. It would be of interest to the committee to know the present policy of the government with regard to power.
The third question has to do with shipbuilding. The minister said the other day that we are launching a merchant ship every four days, and that he hoped that the programme would be accelerated until we were launching a ship every three days. Of course, this merchant shipbuilding is of vital importance to the united nations, and it would seem to be a matter of going the limit-we must build every ship we possibly can. Is it the intention to provide more berths in the present shipbuilding yards, or are new yards to be developed, or what is the policy of the government with regard to the extension of the shipbuilding industry?
In that connection the minister might explain the new government company which has been set up to take charge of the operation of these ships. I think it is called Park Steamships Limited. It would be interesting to know the details as to just what that company is supposed to do, whether it is to operate all the ships that are being built, or whether some are to be turned over to Great Britain. Can the minister give us a report on the developments that have taken place recently along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It has not been the policy of the government to date to invest directly in the development of oil. We have encouraged drilling by permitting a write-off of development expenses of a well before the earnings of the well become taxable, and that has been a stimulant to drilling. We have extended the work of the geological surveys. The government is now in partnership with the government of New Brunswick and is making a thorough investigation of the oil shale deposits in that province. Conversations are going on with regard to the development of the Peace

War Appropriation-Supplies
River area of British Columbia. The government of that province undertook some time ago to develop this field with public funds.
They are still drilling.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: They are still drilling, and it seems to us that while it is a sound way to proceed, perhaps it is too slow to meet the present situation and we are suggesting other means of doing it. We have not arrived at any conclusion, for which reason I will not say much about it. As regards the Alberta tar sands, I do not know whether I can announce a policy at the moment. This field is being thoroughly studied, and we hope to formulate a policy after we have determined what the problem is. There has been a small pilot plant operating on the tar sands, but its operation has never been wholly successful. There are several problems there which have never been worked out in a way to encourage development on a large scale, and one of the principal difficulties is the mining of the sands themselves. That is being extensively studied, and I hope that before the middle of June we shall have a report on it which will enable the government to evolve a policy. The path seems fairly clear, and it is reasonably certain that the government investment will pay, or at least that we shall get something worth while. We may, in the case of the tar sands, invest directly in the development. I offer that as a possibility only, because no decision has been arrived at and the complete facts are not available at the moment.

Considerable survey work
has been going on for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; but the problems have not been worked out. The use of the pilot plant is to help to develop a satisfactory operation which will warrant large scale developments, and while that plant has been in operation there are a good many problems that require further development before a large scale plant will be warranted; that is, a plant running into tens of millions of dollars.
It produced 17,000 barrels last season.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; but that is not very much oil.
That large scale plant would have to be financed by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Probably.

Is the plant at Alexander being operated on an economic
basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: It was burnt down, but my information is that it was never operated on an economic basis. It is a pilot operation. I may say incidentally that a plant of that size has a much better chance of being on an economic basis because the output would be used on the ground. A large development involves transportation to rather distant centres to find a market.
Has the minister taken into consideration the oil shales in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have not studied the shales in Nova Scotia, but we have been studying intensively the oil shales in New Brunswick and, if the results are favourable, we shall look farther on.
Years ago I was a member of the Nova Scotia government, and it was being considered by the department there.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have that in mind for further study. In the matter of depreciation on power developments, I would point out the wartime depreciation board does not come under my jurisdiction. What write-offs there have been, I do not know. I know of no direct capital assistance to power development. I do not know of any write-offs except in the case of the development of the Aluminum Company of Canada, worked out in conjunction with aluminum contracts.
Consolidated too.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; they got a write-off from the wartime depreciation board for development incidental to their work, a development that could not be justified as an ordinary peace-time operation, but which was valuable to the war effort. Ordinarily we have not gone extensively into the development of hydro-electric power.
What is the situation in regard to power?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: All available power is all being used. Every spare kilowatt in Quebec is being taken to Arvida to make aluminum, and that will continue to be the situation. There is no shortage at the moment, but next winter we shall be short of power. Any worth-while hydro development usually takes two years to construct, and we are bringing in about one million horsepower for the next twelve or fourteen months; but even that is spoken for. We shall continue to use every kilowatt we produce, and we shall still be short.

Are there any plans for developing more power?

War Appropriation-Supplies
25S3

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Plans are under way, but not by this government. I have seen an announcement of the Ontario government's scheme, and there are plans for increasing developments at Beauharnois, Shawinigan and one or two other points. I have forgotten what my hon. friend's question was with regard to shipbuilding.

I am not clear whether the government proposes to expand its shipbuilding programme. If it is to be expanded, is it to be done by building new berths in the present yards, or will new yards be developed, or what is the scheme for expanding the shipbuilding industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The industry is constantly expanding. We never close the door on any industry; we are always expanding. We have laid keels in a new six-berth yard within the last week or two in Montreal. We are expanding berths at Vancouver island, and we are also bringing in new berths at Pictou and Sorel. We attempt to fully staff one yard before we start on the next. We have made mistakes; we have opened new shipyards too soon. Once a yard is fully staffed and on a full-time basis-we have only two yards in the country on that basis-it may be worth while to start another yard; but while a yard in a locality is expanding, it is not considered good business-and we were so warned by experts from the United Kingdom-to start another yard. We are expanding at the moment. We have in mind expansions for the future, but no definite plans. Future expansion will depend on how soon we shall be able to fully staff existing yards.
Can the minister give the number of wooden ships being built, boats and vessels, and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The debate seems to have become a general discussion of wooden ships. I thought what we were discussing was wooden cargo ships. It depends on what you call a ship. We have built some 14,000 since the war began, beginning with lifeboats, rowboats, motor launches and up to wooden minesweepers, wooden Fairmiles and all sorts of wooden naval craft. But of wooden cargo ships the number built is zero.
I was thinking of the smaller boats.
What is the situation in regard to wooden mine-sweepers? Is the government building them up to the capacity of the yards, or is it simply a case of ordering a limited number?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
We can hardly build to the capacity of the yards unless somebody is prepared to man the boats when built. The department does not just run wild on a particular type of boat. If, during the next eight months the plan is to train men for, say, twenty boats, we build the twenty boats. Britain may ask us to build fifty for them; we do it. We sell some to the United States. But we cannot build ships just to build ships, except merchant ships; they are a recognized standard type and we are building them as fast as we can. But that is the only type that one might call a readily saleable commodity.
My hon. friend asked about the Park Steamship company. The government is building a number of ships for Canadian operation. It is intended to follow the practice followed in Britain; the government will own the ships, place them for operation in charge of steamship lines that are operating boats in the particular service. For instance, boats to Australia we place for operation with the Manx line; if they are operating to south Africa we would put them perhaps with Furness Withy, or whoever happened to be operating there. The steamship line is paid a small fee for operating the ships and they are operated for the account of the government. All the earnings are paid to the government. The Park Steamship company accepts ownership of these ships on behalf of the government and assigns them to the various lines, attends to the accounting and protects the interest of the government in the operation.
The government itself will not be operating any of these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No.
They will all be operated by private firms?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is right.
Are all those merchant ships to be Canadian ships, or are some to be turned over to Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We are building quite a number for the British government, some for the maritime commission of the United States and some for Canada.
Would it be disclosing information that should not be disclosed if the minister told us the number for Great Britain, for the United States and for Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I would rather not do that. By mutual arrangement we do not disclose any figures in connection with business with the United States. I think it would be unwise. All
War Appropriation-Supplies

I can say is that we are building all the ships we can; we are keeping for Canada as many as we think we can get Canadian crews for, and disposing of the others.

Is there anything in mind
as to what should be done with those Canadian boats at the end of the war, or is that looking too far ahead?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think it is. I do not know what the policy will be. We hope to have them considerably written down by earnings during the war. We may turn them over to the Canadian government merchant marine, or leave them in private hands, or dispose of them outright to private companies. I suppose that is a situation which must be left to the government of that day.

The lines the minister
mentioned as operating these ships are not Canadian lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No; so far as I know, there are no Canadian lines except the Canadian Pacific.
So that at the moment they are practically all being operated by lines owned in other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is right.

About two years ago the Saskatchewan government entered into an arrangement with two joint stock companies to search for oil in Saskatchewan. By virtue of that agreement these companies undertook to spend a certain amount of money, about $400,000, in a seismographic survey of Saskatchewan for oil. I believe that a substantial part of that sum has been expended during the past two years, and that some showings or evidences of oil deposits have been discovered. Within the last few weeks drilling for oil with the most modern equipment obtainable, has commenced at Ceylon, Saskatchewan, and at Radville, Saskatchewan. I believe that the survey for other showings of oil is continuing.
I should like to know from the minister whether, being familiar with that survey and that development, he is satisfied that sufficient progress is being made. I should also be glad to know whether, being familiar with other outcroppings or possibilities, the government would undertake to give some assistance? At a point thirty miles south and a little west of Regina a well was sunk to a depth of 2,500 feet and was not drilled further on account of lack of funds. That well was located as a result of advice from eminent geologists both in this country and across the line. Again, showings of gas have been

found at Shaunavon in southwestern Saskatchewan, at Riverhurst on the Saskatchewan river, at Unity in northwestern Saskatchewan, at Church Bridge in northeastern Saskatchewan; two wells have been drilled at Simpson, ninety miles north of Regina, one to a depth of 3,300 feet and the other to a depth of about 2.000 feet, and I believe a number of wells have been drilled on the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary around Lloydminster. There is a substantial showing of gas and production of low gravity oil. Would the minister consider favourably governmental assistance in finding out whether there are substantial oil deposits at those points?
The minister also referred to an anticipated shortage of power in the coming winter. I understand that in the immediate future Neon lights and other users of electrical energy for purposes not regarded as essential will be substantially curtailed. I gather from what the minister has said that the power development on the Saguenay river will all be required for undertakings now under way. I understand also that it will take about two years to develop the Carillon site in Ontario. Would the minister favourably consider developing the lignite coalfields in Saskatchewan as a source of power? There are twenty billion tons of coal, and that is a lot of coal. The overburden varies in depth from forty to one hundred and fifty feet, and for some ten years now that coal has been mined as a steam shovel proposition. The overburden is cleared by a steam shovel; the coal is picked up by a steam shovel, loaded on flat cars and taken to a plant where it is sized. At the mine mouth an electrical plant has been in operation for ten years.
What grade is the coal?

It is a lignite coal, with
from 7,400 to 7,800 b.t.u. Compared with Alberta or British Columbia coal it is not as good commercially, but power is developed there, and I understand it can be done very cheaply. I understand further that in the United States there is a surplus of steam equipment for producing electricity, due to the fact that many hydro plants have been brought into operation recently as a result of undertakings in the United' States, and these steam plants have been discarded. I do not profess to be an electrical engineer; my knowledge of the subject is most superficial; but I appeal to the minister, who has a practical knowledge of matters of that kind, to learn whether a steam plant of large proportions could not be constructed in Saskatchewan in much less time than would be required for the construction of a hydro plant.

War Appropriation-Supplies
May I assure the minister that if such an enterprise were to be undertaken it would have a definite post-war use. What is most urgently required in Saskatchewan is a large head of power that will be available as an inducement to industrial enterprise to come to that province. As hon. members know, ours is a badly balanced economy, and anything the minister can do consistent with Canada's national war effort to help us to balance our economy will materially assist in settling a very serious post-war problem.

Is
the minister going to have the government do the boring for oil in the Peace River district or, if not, who is going to do it? While I am on my feet I should like also to ask the minister if the government has any intention of constructing an industrial alcohol plant for the production of alcohol to be used together with gasoline. I understand that this is done in England1 and Australia, and that there is a plant in Detroit producing over 12,000 tons a day. Have we any idea of doing anything along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The government has not
developed any oil wells, and I hope it will not be necessary for it to do so while I am minister, because my hon. friend has indicated the difficulties of a minister who undertook to finance oil wells. Of course in time of war the government would not be justified in drilling in anything but a proven field. We are after materials in a hurry, and naturally in spending government money we cannot take too many chances. We do encourage oil companies to drill because they have the experience and the equipment. We have encouraged them, as I say, by tax concessions, with which the committee is familiar. So far we have not gone beyond that. We are very much interested in the Peace River section of British Columbia. We need oil in northern British Columbia, and the reports indicate that the possibilities there are very good. I do not know what we will do, but certainly it will not be a direct government effort, and I doubt whether we shall subsidize a private company. However, we do hope some arrangement can be made to speed up the exploration of that area.

May I ask the minister if at the same time the department is going to look into the oil possibilities at the town of Peace River? Away back in 1921 they had producing wells there but for some reason or another, whether the wells were damaged or interfered with in some way, those wells were capped. That is not very far from the Alaska highway, either. I am told on the best
authority that there is oil at the town of Peace River, and last summer I saw the old wells that were there; I think there are five or six capped wells.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
We have nothing in mind
in that direction. At the moment we are particularly interested in getting all we can out of Turner valley; we are extending the operation at Fort Norman; we want to have a very good look at the Peace river section of British Columbia, and we are making a very thorough examination of the oil shales of New Brunswick to determine their extent and the development that will be necessary. I think that is the extent of our oil explorations at the moment.
And the oil sands also.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, the tar sands; we are going into that very thoroughly, to see what is required there.
With regard to the matter of power, as I have explained we have not invested any money directly in power plants. Two cases have been mentioned to-night in which special depreciation has been authorized by the wartime depreciation board, due to special circumstances, but I do not think the government will invest directly in power plants. I am well aware of the lignite coal situation. I promised the house that we would use a certain amount of lignite coal in our explosives plant at Winnipeg. I tried to buy some this winter, but was unable to do so. I was told by the fuel administrator that this coal was not for me, that it was too badly needed in other places. But I think I can guarantee to take all the coal that can be produced in that area. To build a power plant there, however, would be to overlook a number of other situations that are urgent. Just as in connection with drilling for oil, a government policy of building power plants hither and yon would be a very difficult policy to administer. I think the government will avoid direct investment in power plants. Was there another question I have overlooked?
Industrial alcohol.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
We are producing considerable quantities of industrial alcohol. We are not using it for high test gasoline; we are using alkylate, which is also a petroleum product. We have three large alkylate plants under construction, with one at Calgary nearing completion, but, as my hon. friend knows, industrial alcohol is used in a great number of war operations. We are using a very considerable part of the distillery capacity

War Appropriation-Supplies
of this country to produce industrial alcohol. We will continue to do so, and will continue to expand the operation as the demands increase.

I should like to ask the
minister two questions, one having to do with gasoline and the other with rubber. Gasoline rationing is now in force throughout the country and, generally speaking, I think it has been well received as long as it is applied fairly. But I am wondering if any restrictions have been placed on cities and municipalities to prevent the use of gasoline and oil in the construction of new roads. I am not citing this particularly against the city of Ottawa, because I think this is general throughout the country, but I notice that in connection with the asphalt pavement to be laid in the Riverdale section of Ottawa, it is estimated, according to the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, May 15, that 10,000 gallons of gasoline will be used in the construction of that new piece of asphalt pavement. I may be wrong, but I should think that asphalt pavement will not be in such great demand in the future, because the cars will be fewer in number. It will cause a great deal of heart-burning among those who are curtailed in their use of gasoline, if they see cities and municipalities extending their road-building programmes, and using gasoline and oil in connection therewith. Is there any restriction on cities and municipalities? Have they been prohibited from entering upon extensive programmes?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; there are very severe restrictions. My hon. friend is receiving protests about the use of asphalts, and I am receiving protests from cities which would like to use tarvia. However, they are not permitted to do so, because restrictions are severe with respect to the use of petroleum products on roads. I was surprised to read that asphalt pavements are being laid. I had thought that was prohibited, but I may be wrong. I shall be glad to get the regulations and advise my hon. friend as to what the prohibition is. But tarvia, and products of that kind, cannot be used.

A regulation is in effect, I believe, whereby those having two spare tires have to report the same to the wartime prices and trade board. A request came in to me the other day, and when I made an inquiry from Mr. Williamson's office, who is in charge of rubber control, I was told that a party having two spare tires would have to report to the wartime prices and trade board. My question is this: I am wondering where

this overlapping is going to lead. The wartime prices and trade board have control of the handling of rubber. In a notice issued to-day the whole question of tire rationing is set out. I should like to know what anyone in the wartime prices and trade board has to do with looking after tires. I thought their duty was in connection with prices of various articles. I am pointing out to the committee that we had better keep our eyes on some of these boards, because if you give them an inch they will take ten miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The wartime prices and trade board has charge of the control of peace-time articles, whereas the wartime industries control board deals with strategic materials for war, and the materials necessary for war production. The tire situation is rather involved. Of course rubber is a strategic material for war. It is under the jurisdiction of the controller of supplies, who is attached to the Department of Munitions and Supply. But the enforcement of the regulations has been turned over, by arrangement, to the enforcement officer of the wartime prices and trade board. This board has an enforcement department represented in all parts of the country, under the direction of Mr. McGregor. The enforcement of the rubber rationing regulations is carried out by that branch of the wartime prices and trade board.
The regulation as to trucks is, by arrangement, handled by the wartime prices and trade board-by Mr. Stewart. The regulation of buses, strangely enough, is handled by the transit controller in the Department of Munitions and Supply. There are reasons for each of these divisions. Perhaps one reason why trucks were regulated by the wartime prices and trade board is that I was once bitten and twice shy, and I was not anxious to undertake that branch of control. However, there is a pattern to it, and it seems to be working reasonably well.

I was pleased to hear the minister say that they are investigating the oil shales of New Brunswick, and that there would probably be some developments there. It seems unfortunate that it took a war to bring about those developments, because we have known in New Brunswick for a great many years that we have rich oil shale in that province.
The minister also stated that it was not his intention to develop power plants. I had intended to ask if he would consider enlarging the power plant at Grand Lake in New Brunswick. I understand that one reason why we have not more industries in New Brunswick is our lack of cheaper power, and I believe

War Appropriation-Supplies
this plant could have been developed. An extension could have been made very cheaply and, in justice to my province, I believe we should have more developments there, more munitions plants and other war activities.
However, it was not my intention to speak particularly along that line to-night. There was another matter I wished to bring to the attention of the minister. I believe we have now exhausted the subjects ftf housing, wooden ships and oil. We have also discussed the scarcity of rubber, metal and other commodities, and have considered the provisions being made to see that enough is salvaged for our war needs.
I wish now to ask the minister some questions regarding the scarcity of paper in this country. I would ask first whether there is a scarcity of newsprint and paper? I ask this question knowing the great effort that is being made, from one end of the country to the other, to salvage paper. In every city and every town school children and organizations are gathering up scrap paper. I know that in military camps we are instructed to collect all paper, and as a result every little scrap of paper is collected and saved. I wish the minister would tell us the situation in Canada regarding this commodity. It does seem strange that while we are spending so much time salvaging paper in Canada, we do not seem to have any curtailment in the use of newsprint. I have not noticed that our newspapers are cut down in the quantity of paper they are using. When one buys the Saturday editions of newspapers he will find that they consist of forty or fifty pages, and I believe that in war time five or six pages would be sufficient. It is a strange anomaly that every schoolboy in every community is being asked to salvage paper, while at the same time we permit this great waste of paper throughout the country. I believe the government is setting a good example in many cases by using both sides of paper in its correspondence. Orderly rooms at military camps are instructed to use both sides of the paper in preparing their orders. Everything is being done to try to save paper, and we are told that such saving is necessary because paper is scarce.
Another matter which might very well be mentioned at this time is the export of paper from Canada. If there is a scarcity of newsprint, why is it that a paper such as the Chicago Tribune can have exported from Canada thousands of tons of paper used in the publication of that newspaper which, as hon. members know, was anti-British before the United States entered the war? It never loses an opportunity even now to disparage
our own Canadian effort in the war. It disparages the efforts of Great Britain and of the whole British empire, and still we in Canada are exporting a commodity which must be scarce. If it is not, then why do we have these provisions for the collection of salvage and scrap paper?
These are questions I should like the minister to answer. I have hesitated to bring them to his attention at so late an hour in the day. After such a long and trying day, however, possibly these questions will appear much easier to answer than some which were propounded to him this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes. As a matter of fact I have enjoyed the discussion very much. I am glad to give what information I can on the subject. I think there is a misunderstanding as to why campaigns for the collection of paper are necessary. This is not done because of a shortage of newsprint for the purposes for which newsprint is usually used. As a matter of fact there is spare capacity for the production of newsprint, because some of our mills are working only four or five days a week. But there is a great need for pulp or rough cardboard, wood pulp pressed into sheets for the packing of shells and finished rounds of ammunition. Newspapers or paper of any kind are just as good for that purpose as pulp made from newly cut timber. It is really to save a drain on our lumber mills and to prevent waste that we are collecting newspapers and using them for that purpose. I do not know whether there would be a shortage of paper if we had to use freshly cut pulp for packing shells, but there very likely would be. At the moment we are able to fill our own needs for newsprint, satisfy the export demand and still have some surplus capacity. Nevertheless I want to impress upon all hon. members that the salvage campaign for old paper is well worth considering.
As far as writing paper goes, there was a shortage of that at one time and it may still exist. I believe the campaign to use both sides of a sheet of paper for official documents is worth while, and I think it will carry on after the war. I see no reason why we should write only on the one side of a sheet of paper, and I think this habit of thrift is well worth cultivating.
As far as the oil shales of New Brunswick are concerned, my hon. friend probably knows that they were under private control for a long time. It was only after they were restored to the control of the province that it was worth while for governments to spend considerable sums of money investigating them.

There has been a great deal of discussion to-night about oil shales. Among the many other things that we have in British Columbia are some deposits of oil shale. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister who brought it to the attention of the oil controller. He wrote me to say that he had investigated it last summer when on the coast, and he did not think there was very much in it. However, apparently some one in the department has changed their minds since then because I have a letter from the assistant oil controller asking me where further information can be obtained. I am glad to know that this matter will be investigated.
In connection with gasoline I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), that we should accept these restrictions, not reluctantly but with good grace in order to assist the government to conserve gasoline for the purposes we have in hand, and that none should be wasted for pleasure purposes while there is a need for our war effort. One of the difficulties that I find in getting people to see the necessity for saving gasoline is the fact that the regulations do not seem to operate equitably. I have received several letters about this, and I have one from a man who has a light delivery truck. He tells me that he has a wife and four children and, since he cannot afford a private car, he takes his family out in the truck on Sundays to the beaches or other places. It was intimated to him that he could not use his truck for driving around on Sundays, that he might have his permit cancelled if he did so. He feels rather badly about this. He states that if he could afford a private car he could get a category A card for it and use it on Sundays. He enclosed the letter he received from the regional office manager for the oil controller in Vancouver. This letter was most reasonable, and I think I should read it. It reads:
I have your letter of April 30 and although as yet there are no specific regulations which prohibit the use of your panel delivery truck for personal driving, I must point out to you that the commercial category books have been assigned to you for commercial purposes and in view of the serious shortage of gasoline you are not expected to drive such long distances as from here to White Rock and return for private purposes any more than the owner of a passenger automobile.
Are owners of private automobiles going to be restricted from driving long distances? Of course, if they do drive long distances their ration cards will not go so far. If some

way could be found whereby people who cannot afford a private car, or two or three cars, can be made to feel that they are not being discriminated against while other people in better circumstances are allowed their ordinary pleasures, I think it would be much easier. I do not know just how that could be done, but if it could be done it would help a great deal.
I should like to say a word on the matter of saving paper. I think a great deal of paper would be saved if there were less advertising. There is a lot of what appears to me to be the most useless kind of advertising, and I am sure it comes to every hon. member in reams. I have before me an advertisement by the Firestone Rubber company. They have no commercial rubber to sell because I imagine the government takes it all for war purposes, but yet here is a most expensive' advertisement, on expensive paper in colours. This all takes time and materials; it needs skilled labour to produce, and it seems to me that we are not putting everything into our war effort when we allow what appears to be waste. I saw an article recently, I think it was in the Financial Post, to the effect that the Aluminum Company of Canada, although it did not have a pot or a pan or any other article of aluminum to sell, had provided an appropriation of $1,000,000 this year to advertise these articles. I also have under my hand a full-page advertisement by Dominion Foundries and Steel Limited, Hamilton, Canada, which appeared in the Financial Post. These people do not need to advertise their wares at the present time. It takes time and it consumes materials to put out such advertising. There are many ways that we have not touched yet in which we can save waste and add to the efficiency of the work we have in hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, every effort is being made to eliminate unfairness in rationing. I was told-in fact the gentleman concerned himself told me-of a motorist who was driving out of Toronto some time ago when he was stopped by an enforcement officer, who asked where he was going. He said he was going fishing. Where was he going? He gave the destination. The enforcement officer asked to see his category, found that he was in category C, and pointed out to him that that was a business category for business purposes, and that if he could go fishing on that category he did not need a C rating. The next day his book was exchanged for a category A book.
We are trying to bring all those who use their cars for pleasure into category A. In

War Appropriation-Supplies
fact it is quite possible that there will be a category lower than A for people who use cars exclusively for pleasure. We are trying to eliminate unfairness; that is, we are not giving high categories to people who do a good deal of pleasure driving.
Whether we like it or not, pleasure driving is going to be a real luxury. Gasoline is for those who have a real use for it in connection with the war effort. We are going to try to take care of people who must go to war plants; business executives; producers in the war effort, such as farmers, and other people who have a real need for gasoline. But the man who simply drives from here to there for pleasure is going to be without gasoline shortly.
So, I think, my hon. friend's acquaintance who had the truck was simply getting the same kind of treatment that the man in a business category who is using his car for pleasure is getting as the enforcement officers catch up with him.

What about the man with two cars in the family? I suppose that will be checked, too. I know of people who have two cars in a single family, and while I doubt whether their business entitles them to better than category 1A, through some agency they have obtained category C.
The other day I asked for an extension of the hours of sales of gasoline to farmers. I am pleased that the minister announced today that this request had been granted.
I also spoke of a certain oil company-I think I had better mention that it was the British-American-trucking their own products from Moose Jaw through southeastern Saskatchewan and southern Manitoba. Since I spoke on this matter I have had a letter from the secretary of one of those towns pointing out that in twenty-four hours ten very large trucks with trailers went through that town. He estimated that those trucks used fifty gallons a day; they had very heavy tires on their trucks and trailers, and they were paralleling a railway line. The Canadian Pacific railway agent there tells me that they can obtain tankers along that line. Also the man-power situation comes into the matter, because each of those trucks requires a driver, whereas the use of a tank car on the railway would eliminate that. To what extent this practice is carried on I do not know, but it is a serious wastage. Further, it sets a bad example to the people in those towns, who wonder why they should curtail their own small supplies while those companies are
allowed to carry on in this way. I trust the minister will look into the practice and prohibit it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The matter of trucking oil was mentioned in this chamber a while ago, and at that time I sent a marked copy of Hansard to the controller for his action.

I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Regina City in the excellent appeal he made for our province with reference to having a part to play in the economic aspect of our war effort. The hour is too late for me to say very much about the matter now, but it seems to me that there are two factors to which some attention might be directed.
The first is the one he has mentioned, and to which the minister has already replied-the possibility of developing power, either in the north, where we have considerable water power, or in the south where there are very large coal deposits. I can appreciate the point of view expressed by the minister. Nevertheless there is a strong feeling that a greater use could be made of the industrial resources of the prairie, rather than draining off the population, as has happened in the last year or two.
The other factor in the contribution which we might make has to do with the bits-and-pieces programme of the department. The minister has not made any detailed statement on it, and it is too late to-night, but I wonder if he would do so to-morrow. This afternoon he made a statement with reference to garage-men. He said that provision would be made for the type of establishment which was equipped to do something. My understanding of the set-up does not lead me to believe that that is taking place. Mr. Pyne, who has been handling the subcontract coordination branch in Winnipeg for western Canada, does not, I understand, place subcontracts direct from the government; he acts as a sort of employment agent for firms who have contracts and want to know of people who can take subcontracts. He does not place contracts; he only directs firms which have contracts to people who might take subcontracts. I believe that they are not making full use of the people who could be doing more in our bits-and-pieces programme. I am not going to take time to elaborate that to-night. I know that a survey was made of the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. When I was west I saw a copy of the survey. I hesitate to quote from it from memory, but I believe there are 277 machine tools which were listed in the two provinces and which were not being used.
Questions

They would, of course, vary in size. I know a number of such cases. One man in particular with a small aluminum foundry has done some excellent work. But these people do not seem to have been able to make any contacts. They go to Mr. Pyne, who says, "I should be very glad to give you something to do, and as soon as some firm asks us for a subcontractor we will direct them to you." But that is not very satisfactory, and for two years these people have been twiddling their thumbs; either they have to move east and get a job there, or stay where they are and continue to do commercial work.
I would appreciate it if the minister would give us to-morrow some outline of the bits-and-pieces programme, whether it is his intention to expand it, and how it would be possible for these men who think they can play some part in Canada's industrial effort to be brought more directly in contact with the government and those places where there are contracts.
Progress reported.
